findings.title: No tax computation path exists for a company, firm or LLP — the entity-rate and MAT/AMT engines are reachable from no router and no screen
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/entity_rates.py:141 compute_entity_tax() and apps/api/domain/income_tax/minimum_tax.py:145 compute_mat / :177 compute_amt are complete and well-tested. `grep -rn "from domain.income_tax" --include=*.py apps/api | grep -v tests/ | grep -v domain/income_tax/` returns importers for itr_engine, statutory_rates, capital_gains_engine, advance_tax_interest_engine, computation_workspace, itr_workflow, form26as_service — and NOTHING for entity_rates, minimum_tax, presumptive, regime_election, book_to_tax_bridge, itr_json or itr_schema. The only computation endpoint is apps/api/routers/income_tax.py:113 POST /api/income-tax/compute, whose request model (routers/income_tax.py:62 ComputeITRRequest) has no entity field at all and whose engine (domain/income_tax/itr_engine.py:236 ITREngine.compute) only ever applies individual slabs via _slabs_for (itr_engine.py:485).
findings.ca_experience: A CA opens Client → Income Tax → Tax Computation for a Private Limited company, types in the profit, and gets tax computed on the INDIVIDUAL new-regime slab table — nil up to ₹4 lakh, 5% to ₹8 lakh, with a ₹60,000 §87A rebate. A company pays 22%/25%/30% from the first rupee and gets no rebate. On the live book described in CLAUDE.md (4 Private Limited, 1 LLP, 1 Partnership, 1 Proprietorship, zero individuals) the one computation endpoint the product has fits none of the clients. MAT under §115JB — the exact case of large book profit and small taxable income — is never charged.
findings.market_standard: Winman, CompuTax, Genius, Saral and TaxCloud all compute for every assessee class from one screen: individual, HUF, firm, LLP, company (normal / §115BAA / §115BAB), AOP/BOI and trust, with MAT/AMT and the §115JAA/§115JD credit register carried year to year.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an assessee_kind to ComputeITRRequest and branch in ITREngine: individuals to the slab path, firm/LLP/company to compute_entity_tax, then apply_minimum_tax over the result. Expose the company regime and the turnover-reference-year figure (entity_rates.turnover_reference_fy) as inputs, and persist the MAT/AMT credit generated on the snapshot.

findings.title: A capital LOSS entered as a negative figure reduces slab tax on salary — §71(3) set-off restriction is not applied
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/itr_engine.py:394 `stcg_tax = req.capital_gains_stcg_paise * rates.stcg_111a_rate_bps // 10000` — no max(0, …); same at :397 and :399. The negative also enters `gti` at :316 and `taxable_income` at :382. routers/income_tax.py:84-86 declares capital_gains_stcg_paise / ltcg_paise / ltcg_other_paise as plain `int = 0` with no `ge=0`. Probe run this session: salary ₹20,00,000 alone → total tax ₹1,92,400; the same salary with capital_gains_stcg_paise = −₹5,00,000 → total tax ₹88,400.
findings.ca_experience: A CA who records a ₹5 lakh short-term capital loss the natural way — as a negative — sees the client's tax on ₹20 lakh of salary fall by ₹1,04,000. IT Act §71(3) allows a capital loss to be set off only against capital gains, never against salary; §74 carries the balance forward. The return understates tax by six figures and looks entirely reasonable on screen.
findings.market_standard: Every ITR utility (and Winman/CompuTax) keeps capital losses in Schedule CG and Schedule CFL, sets them off only inside the capital-gains head in the statutory order, and carries the balance forward for eight years. None of them lets a capital loss touch salary.
findings.suggested_fix: Clamp each capital-gains tax component with max(0, …) so a negative can never produce negative tax; exclude negative gains from `ordinary_income` and `gti`; add `ge=0` to the three router fields and take losses through a separate, explicit brought-forward/current-year capital-loss input that only nets within the head.

findings.title: §80G is allowed in full at 50% or 100% with no qualifying limit of 10% of adjusted gross total income and no cash-donation cap
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/itr_engine.py:127-130 — `Donation80G.eligible_paise()` is simply `amount_paise * deduction_pct // 100`; the value is summed at itr_engine.py:352 (`d80g = sum(d.eligible_paise() ...)`) and added straight to deductions with no reference to gross total income. routers/income_tax.py:54 constrains deduction_pct to 50..100 only. Probe: salary ₹10,00,000, one donation of ₹9,00,000 at 50% → deduction_80g_paise = ₹4,50,000, taxable income ₹5,00,000.
findings.ca_experience: A CA entering a ₹9 lakh donation for a client with ₹10 lakh of salary is shown a ₹4,50,000 deduction. §80G(4) caps the qualifying amount for donations in the 'subject to qualifying limit' category at 10% of adjusted GTI — about ₹95,000 here, so ₹47,500 of deduction. The computation overstates the deduction by roughly ₹4 lakh and the client's return will be reduced on processing under §143(1). §80G(5D) also disallows any cash donation above ₹2,000 entirely — not modelled.
findings.market_standard: ClearTax, Winman and the ITD utility itself all classify each donation into the four §80G buckets (100% without limit, 50% without limit, 100% subject to limit, 50% subject to limit), compute adjusted GTI, apply the 10% cap to the limited buckets only, and refuse cash donations over ₹2,000.
findings.suggested_fix: Give Donation80G a bucket enum and a payment mode. Compute adjusted GTI (GTI less LTCG/STCG-111A, less other Chapter VI-A deductions), apply the 10% cap to the two limited buckets, and disallow cash above ₹2,000 with a named reason. Add a test that fails against the current code for the ₹9L-on-₹10L case.

verification.probe: ran ITREngine.compute: 9L donation at 50% on 10L salary gave a 4,50,000 deduction

findings.title: The capital-gains engine ignores the date of transfer, so every pre-23-July-2024 sale is charged at Budget-2024 rates
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/capital_gains_engine.py:160-178 — the equity branch returns rate 20.0 for STCG and 12.5% with a ₹1,25,000 exemption for LTCG unconditionally; `sale_date` is used only for holding-period arithmetic (:103) and for the CII lookup (:143). No branch anywhere in the file reads 23-07-2024. Probe: compute_capital_gains('equity', purchase 10-Jan-2024, sale 10-Jun-2024, cost ₹10L, sale ₹15L) → 20.0%, tax ₹1,00,000; the statutory rate for a transfer before 23-07-2024 is 15% under §111A, i.e. ₹75,000. Probe: LTCG on equity sold 10-Jun-2024 with a ₹20L gain → ₹2,34,375 at 12.5%; §112A charged 10% for that transfer, i.e. ₹1,87,500.
findings.ca_experience: FY 2024-25 work is live now — belated and revised returns for AY 2025-26, updated returns under §139(8A) for earlier years, and any reassessment. A CA computing a client's April-to-July 2024 share sales is handed a figure a third too high on STCG and a quarter too high on LTCG, with no warning. The number is also PERSISTED: POST /api/income-tax/capital-gains (routers/income_tax.py:353) writes result.tax_rate_percent into the capital_gains register.
findings.market_standard: Every Indian tax package split the FY 2024-25 capital-gains schedule at 23 July 2024 the season it happened — the ITD's own Schedule CG has separate before/after 23.07.2024 rows for §111A, §112A and §112, precisely because the rate depends on the transfer date, not the year.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the rate table date-versioned rather than FY-versioned for capital gains: a `rates_for_transfer(sale_date)` that returns 15%/10%/20%-with-indexation before 23-07-2024 and 20%/12.5%/12.5% on and after, with the ₹1.25L §112A exemption applying to the whole of FY 2024-25. Refuse rather than guess for years whose rates are not held.

verification.probe: ran compute_capital_gains for a 10-Jun-2024 transfer: 20% STCG / 12.5% LTCG, i.e. post-23-07-2024 rates

findings.title: The per-client Tax Computation workspace collects only five figures — no deductions, no house property, no capital gains — so an old-regime individual is computed with zero Chapter VI-A relief
findings.evidence: apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/computation/page.tsx:200-233 — the compute payload is exactly gross_salary_paise, business_income_paise, disallowances_paise, other_income_paise, tds_deducted_paise, advance_tax_paid_paise and use_new_regime. The backend request model (apps/api/routers/income_tax.py:62-110) accepts house_property_income_paise, all three capital-gains heads, s80c, s80d, donations_80g, hra, home_loan_interest_24b_paise, nps_80ccd1b_paise, savings_interest_80tta_paise, employer_nps_80ccd2_paise, is_senior_citizen and other_deductions_paise — none of which this screen sends. The only screen that does send them, apps/web/app/income-tax/deductions/page.tsx:222-262, is a firm-level planner with no link to the client's snapshot.
findings.ca_experience: A CA preparing an old-regime individual return in the client workspace types salary and TDS and gets a tax figure computed with a ₹50,000 standard deduction and nothing else — no §80C, no §80D, no HRA, no §24(b), no senior-citizen slab. findings.market_standard: Winman, CompuTax and ClearTax present the full computation sheet — all five heads, every Chapter VI-A section, Schedule CG, Schedule HP with the let-out/self-occupied split — on the client's own screen, and the regime comparison is a column in that same sheet rather than a separate planner.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the five-field form with the full ComputeITRRequest surface on the client workspace screen, and make the deductions planner write into the same snapshot rather than into tax_planning_records.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The client-workspace computation screen sends only five money figures plus regime, so an old-regime computation there gets the ₹50,000 standard deduction and nothing else, and the deduction-free figure is saved as the snapshot the ITR filing demo reads (apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/computation/page.tsx:222-256; apps/api/services/filing_demo/itr.py:52-97). findings.title: §234C interest is charged on the first three instalments for a §44AD/§44ADA presumptive assessee, who owes none
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/advance_tax_interest_engine.py:78-83 INSTALLMENT_RULES applies the 15/45/75/100 four-instalment schedule to every caller; the module header (lines 22-32) says the presumptive single-instalment case is 'out of scope here'. compute_234c_interest (:135) has no assessee parameter and routers/income_tax.py:497 ComputeAdvanceTaxRequest has no field for one. Probe: estimated tax ₹1,00,000 paid in full on 15-Mar-2026 → instalments 1/2/3 each shown short, interest ₹450 + ₹1,350 + ₹2,250 = ₹4,050.
findings.ca_experience: A doctor or a small trader filing under §44AD/§44ADA legitimately pays the whole advance tax by 15 March. The proviso to §211(1) makes that one instalment the whole liability and §234C(1)(b) charges interest only if the 15 March payment falls short. The screen tells the CA the client owes ₹4,050 of interest that is not due, on a client segment CLAUDE.md itself says is a large part of an Indian practice's book. The reverse error is worse in the other direction: a §44AD client shown a 15 June 'shortfall' may be advised to pay early for no reason.
findings.market_standard: Winman, CompuTax and ClearTax all take a 'presumptive u/s 44AD/44ADA' flag on the advance-tax screen and collapse the schedule to one 15-March instalment with the §234C(1)(b) rule.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an `is_presumptive_44ad_44ada` flag to compute_234c_interest and to the endpoint; when set, use a single rule (100% by 15 March, 1 month, no tolerance) and say so in the response.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The §234C engine applies the four-instalment schedule to every assessee and the module itself says the §44AD/§44ADA single-15-March-instalment case is out of scope (apps/api/domain/income_tax/advance_tax_interest_engine.py:66-83), yet neither the function (:128) nor the endpoint model (apps/api/routers/income_tax.py:480) can express it, so a presumptive client who pays in full on 15 March is shown interest on instalments 1-3 that the proviso to §211(1) does not make due.
verification.probe: venv/bin/python -c "compute_234c_interest('2025-26', 100_00_000, [InstallmentPayment(4, 100_00_000, date(2026,3,15))])" printed instalments 1/2/3 short with interest 45000/135000/225000 paise and TOTAL 405000 paise = ₹4,050; instalment 4 ok.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed, with one citation correction: the 'out of scope here' sentence about presumptive assessees is at apps/api/domain/income_tax/advance_tax_interest_engine.py:66-73 (the comment above INSTALLMENT_RULES), not lines 22-32 (which are about treating §234C's numeric structure as settled). The substance holds: INSTALLMENT_RULES at :78-83 is the 15/45/75/100 four-instalment table, compute_234c_interest at :128 takes only (fy, estimated_tax_paise, payments) with no assessee parameter, and ComputeAdvanceTaxRequest at apps/api/routers/income_tax.py:480-483 has no presumptive flag either.
lens_notes.guards: None found. grep for '44AD|presumptive' in apps/web/app/income-tax/advance-tax/page.tsx returns nothing; the page's own header comment (lines 3-6) restates the four-instalment schedule as universal. No test pins a presumptive case.
lens_notes.reach: Fully reachable. apps/web/app/income-tax/advance-tax/page.tsx:132 calls computeAdvanceTaxInterest → apps/web/lib/data/income-tax.ts:391-392 → POST /api/income-tax/advance-tax/compute, and income_tax.router is mounted at apps/api/main.py:267. The page is linked from the income-tax hub (apps/web/app/income-tax/page.tsx:738, 1033).

findings.title: AMT surcharge for an individual or HUF uses the partnership firm's 12%-above-₹1-crore ladder instead of the individual surcharge brackets
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/minimum_tax.py:224-227 — compute_amt calls apply_surcharge_with_marginal_relief with `entity.firm_surcharge` for EVERY non-corporate assessee, individuals and HUFs included; entity_rates.py:88 defines firm_surcharge as a single SurchargeBracket(1 crore, 12%). The individual ladder (10/15/25/37 with the 25% new-regime cap) lives in statutory_rates.py:140-146 and is never consulted here. Probe: individual with adjusted total income ₹3,00,00,000 → AMT before surcharge ₹55,50,000, surcharge ₹6,66,000 (12%); the individual bracket above ₹2 crore is 25%. At ₹80,00,000 the surcharge computed is ₹0; an individual above ₹50 lakh owes 10%.
findings.ca_experience: An individual or HUF who has claimed §10AA or §35AD and falls into AMT has the surcharge on the minimum tax understated by 13 percentage points at ₹3 crore — about ₹7.2 lakh plus cess — and by the whole 10% at ₹80 lakh. The return under-reports the minimum tax and the shortfall surfaces as a §143(1) adjustment with §234B interest.
findings.market_standard: Winman and CompuTax compute AMT surcharge on the assessee's own First-Schedule ladder — the same one that governs their regular tax — because §115JC's charge is on the person, not on a firm-shaped default.
findings.suggested_fix: Select the surcharge brackets by assessee inside compute_amt: individual/HUF/AOP/BOI/AJP → statutory_rates.surcharge_brackets (with the 25% cap where §115BAC applies), firm/LLP → firm_surcharge.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The code defect is real — compute_amt uses the firm's 12% bracket for individuals and HUFs (apps/api/domain/income_tax/minimum_tax.py:225-227 with entity_rates.py:85) — but minimum_tax.py is dead code: no router, service or screen calls it (only tests/test_minimum_tax.py does), so the 'return under-reports the minimum tax' consequence in the finding does not occur. Worth fixing before AMT is ever wired up, not before.
verification.probe: venv/bin/python -c "compute_amt(adjusted_total_income_paise=..., assessee='individual', claimed_specified_deduction=True, fy='2025-26')" printed: ₹80,00,000 → surcharge ₹0; ₹3,00,00,000 → base ₹55,50,000, surcharge ₹6,66,000 (12%), total ₹64,64,640. Matches the finding's numbers.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed exactly. apps/api/domain/income_tax/minimum_tax.py:225-227 calls apply_surcharge_with_marginal_relief(base, tax, entity.firm_surcharge, None, ...) for every non-corporate assessee — individual, HUF, AOP, BOI and artificial juridical person included (the company branch has already returned at :197-203). entity.firm_surcharge is the single 12%-above-₹1-crore bracket at apps/api/domain/income_tax/entity_rates.py:85; the individual ladder 10/15/25/37 with the new-regime 25% cap is at apps/api/domain/income_tax/statutory_rates.py:146-153 and is never consulted in this module.
lens_notes.guards: No test pins AMT surcharge for an individual — apps/api/tests/test_minimum_tax.py only asserts surcharge behaviour for the company MAT case (:36-39) and the firm/LLP effective rate (:72-77); the individual tests (:110-121) exercise only the §115JEE threshold. So there is no test either catching the bug or recording it as deliberate.
lens_notes.reach: This is the decisive lens and it refutes the finding's stated consequence. grep across apps/api for 'minimum_tax|compute_amt|115JC' outside the module and its own tests returns exactly one hit — a comment in apps/api/domain/income_tax/itr_json.py:112. No router imports minimum_tax, no service calls compute_amt, and nothing in apps/web references AMT/§115JC. The module is exercised only by tests, so no return under-reports anything and no CA sees this surcharge today.

findings.title: The unexhausted basic exemption limit is never absorbed against §111A / §112 capital gains, so a small resident taxpayer is over-taxed several times over
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/itr_engine.py:392-399 computes stcg_tax, ltcg_tax and ltcg_other_tax on the raw gain figures with no reference to ordinary income or to the slab's nil band; the only reduction applied is the ₹1,25,000 §112A exemption at :396. Probe: a resident with ONLY ₹5,00,000 of §111A short-term gain and no other income → total tax ₹1,04,000. The proviso to §111A(1) reduces the gain by the amount by which total income (as reduced by that gain) falls short of the maximum amount not chargeable to tax — ₹4,00,000 under §115BAC for FY 2025-26 — leaving ₹1,00,000 at 20% ≈ ₹20,800. Same shape on the LTCG probe: ₹5,00,000 of §112A gain alone → ₹48,750 charged.
findings.ca_experience: A retired client or a homemaker whose only income for the year is a share sale is shown five times the tax actually payable. This is a common real case in an SME practice and the CA has no way to make the screen produce the right figure.
findings.market_standard: The ITD's own utility and every commercial package apply the proviso automatically for a resident individual/HUF and show the absorbed exemption as a line in Schedule SI.
findings.suggested_fix: After computing ordinary_taxable, compute the unused nil band for the applicable slab table and, for a resident individual/HUF, reduce §111A and §112 gains by that shortfall in the statutory order before applying the special rates. Cite the proviso to §111A(1) and to §112(1)(a)(ii)/(b)(ii) in the code.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The ITR engine genuinely never absorbs the unused basic exemption against §111A/§112/§112A gains (apps/api/domain/income_tax/itr_engine.py:378-399) and returns the inflated figures the finding quotes, but no screen sends capital-gains figures to that endpoint, so the 'retired client is shown five times the tax' scenario is unreachable until the workspace form (IT-05) grows capital-gains inputs. It is a latent wrong number, not one a CA sees today.
verification.probe: venv/bin/python -c "ITREngine().compute(...)" printed: STCG-only ₹5,00,000 → total tax ₹1,04,000; §112A-only ₹5,00,000 → ₹48,750; §112-other-only ₹5,00,000 → ₹65,000. New-regime nil band is ₹4,00,000 (statutory_rates.py:115), so the proviso would leave ₹1,00,000 taxable.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed. apps/api/domain/income_tax/itr_engine.py:394-399 charges stcg_tax, ltcg_tax and ltcg_other_tax on the raw head figures; the only reduction is the ₹1,25,000 §112A exemption at :395. ordinary_taxable is computed at :378 and never consulted when taxing the special-rate heads, so the unexhausted nil band of the slab table is not absorbed. grep for 'basic exemption|maximum amount not chargeable|unexhausted' across apps/api finds no implementation anywhere (only unrelated payroll/presumptive prose).
lens_notes.guards: None — no test asserts the proviso, and the engine emits no warning. The separate per-asset calculator apps/api/domain/income_tax/capital_gains_engine.py:142-180 has the same absence, but it is a single-transaction estimator that structurally cannot know the taxpayer's other income, so it is not the same defect.
lens_notes.reach: This is where the finding overstates. Only two screens call POST /api/income-tax/compute — apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/computation/page.tsx:222 and apps/web/app/income-tax/deductions/page.tsx:269-270 — and NEITHER sends any capital_gains_* field (see IT-05). apps/api/routers/itr_workspace.py, domain/income_tax/computation_workspace.py and itr_json.py contain no capital-gains handling at all (grep 'capital_gain|stcg|ltcg' returns nothing). So a CA cannot today produce the over-taxed figure through the product; the field exists on the API and on the frontend type (apps/web/lib/data/income-tax.ts:54-56) but nothing populates it.

findings.title: IT Act §32 depreciation (block of assets, WDV, the 180-day half-rate rule, additional depreciation) is implemented nowhere, so the book-to-tax bridge can never complete for a business client
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/book_to_tax_bridge.py:22-38 states it plainly and refuses rather than defaulting; build_bridge (:129) marks the bridge incomplete when depreciation_under_section_32_paise is None. `grep -rni 'block of assets|block_of_assets' --include=*.py apps/api/domain apps/api/routers apps/api/services` returns only that docstring. apps/api/routers/fixed_assets.py:6-41 computes Companies Act Schedule II SL/WDV depreciation per asset and holds _DEFAULT_WDV_RATES for that Act only. The bridge itself is also imported by no router (see IT-01 evidence).
findings.ca_experience: For every company, firm and proprietorship client — which is the whole of the described live book — the largest single line in the computation sheet has to be worked out on paper or in Excel and typed in, and there is no screen to type it into because build_bridge is not exposed. A CA cannot produce the statement of total income that an assessing officer asks for from this product.
findings.market_standard: Tally Prime, Winman, CompuTax and Genius all maintain a parallel §32 block register — blocks at 15/30/40%, additions split by the 180-day rule, sale proceeds reduced from the block, additional depreciation under §32(1)(iia) — alongside the Companies Act register, and print the depreciation schedule for Clause 18 of Form 3CD.
findings.suggested_fix: Build a §32 block register beside the fixed-asset register (blocks, opening WDV, additions before/after 180 days, deletions, block rate, unabsorbed depreciation), and expose build_bridge behind an endpoint that reads it. Keep the refusal for any block a human has not classified.

verification.what_is_actually_true: IT Act §32 block depreciation (blocks, opening WDV, the 180-day half-rate split, additional depreciation) exists nowhere in the codebase, and the one module that would consume it, apps/api/domain/income_tax/book_to_tax_bridge.py:84-139, is reachable from no router or screen — so the largest adjustment in a business client's statement of total income has to be produced outside the product entirely.

findings.title: Tax audit is a four-field tracker: no Form 3CD at all, and the §44AB applicability test is decided in TypeScript by amount rather than by the client's own business/profession status
findings.evidence: apps/web/app/income-tax/tax-audit/page.tsx is the whole feature — a row per client with form_type, status, auditor, dates, UDIN and turnover, written straight to the tax_audits table over PostgREST (:150-163). Thresholds live in apps/web/lib/income-tax/taxAuditThresholds.ts, whose own header records that the ₹10 crore and ₹75 lakh cash-test limits are 'not modeled here'. page.tsx:207-213 then decides the message purely by size: `turnover >= ₹1cr ? 'mandatory (business)' : turnover >= ₹50L ? 'mandatory (profession)' : ...`. `grep -rni '3cd|3ca|3cb' --include=*.py apps/api` finds only an engagement-letter template and a compliance-obligation label — no clause data anywhere.
findings.ca_experience: A trader with ₹60 lakh turnover is told '✓ Exceeds ₹50 lakh — tax audit mandatory (profession)'. No audit applies. A business with ₹5 crore turnover and under 5% cash receipts and payments is told the audit is mandatory when the first proviso to §44AB(a) raises its threshold to ₹10 crore. And once the CA does have a real audit, the product holds none of Form 3CD — not one of its forty-plus clauses — so the actual deliverable is produced elsewhere.
findings.market_standard: Winman, CompuTax, Genius and TaxCloud generate the complete 3CA/3CB-3CD from the books: Clause 18 depreciation, Clause 21 disallowances, Clause 26 §43B, Clause 34 TDS reconciliation, Clause 44 GST expenditure break-up, plus the UDIN field and the JSON for the portal. A tax-audit tracker with no 3CD is a spreadsheet.
findings.suggested_fix: Move the §44AB test to the backend, take business-vs-profession from the client record and the cash-receipts/cash-payments percentages as inputs, and return a reasoned applicability answer. Then build 3CD as a clause workspace fed by the existing disallowance, TDS and GST data.

findings.title: §234A and §234B are implemented and tested but exposed by no endpoint and no screen — only §234C reaches a CA
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/advance_tax_interest_engine.py:239 compute_234a_interest and :306 compute_234b_interest are complete. apps/api/routers/income_tax.py:22 imports only `compute_234c_interest, installment_schedule, InstallmentPayment, INSTALLMENT_RULES`; `grep -rn 'compute_234a|compute_234b' apps/api/routers apps/api/services` returns nothing, and `grep -rn '234A|234B' apps/web/app apps/web/lib` finds only prose in the payroll reports page. The advance-tax screen (apps/web/app/income-tax/advance-tax/page.tsx:220) shows a single 'Interest u/s 234C' figure. There is also no self-assessment tax / Challan 280 capture anywhere.
findings.ca_experience: A client who files late owes §234A at 1% a month on the net tax, and one who paid under 90% of assessed tax owes §234B from 1 April of the assessment year — usually the LARGER of the three interest charges. The product computes neither, so the 'net payable' figure on the computation screen and on the snapshot is understated for every late or under-paid return, and the CA has to work them out by hand before paying the self-assessment tax.
findings.market_standard: Winman, CompuTax and ClearTax compute 234A/234B/234C together as one interest block on the computation sheet and roll them into the self-assessment tax payable, with the challan captured against the return.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a /api/income-tax/interest endpoint returning all three sections, feed it the filing date and the assessment date, surface the block on the client computation screen, and add a self-assessment tax / challan field so the payload's self_assessment_tax figure has a source.

findings.title: Holding period is counted in whole calendar months rather than days, so a holding one day short of twelve months is classified long-term
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/capital_gains_engine.py:103-105 — `holding_months` is `(sale.year-buy.year)*12 + (sale.month-buy.month)`, with the day of the month discarded; is_long_term (:107) compares that count against 12 or 24. Probe: purchase 15-Jan-2024, sale 05-Jan-2025 → holding_months 12, is_long_term True, rate 12.5%. Actual holding is 356 days, so §2(42A) makes it SHORT term at 20% under §111A. tests/test_capital_gains_engine.py:38-40 pins this behaviour rather than catching it.
findings.ca_experience: A share sold a few days before the twelve-month anniversary is taxed at 12.5% instead of 20%, and the misclassification is written into the capital_gains register (routers/income_tax.py:371 stores `gain_type`). The error runs both ways at the 24-month boundary for property. On a ₹20 lakh gain the difference is ₹1.5 lakh, and it is the kind of thing a scrutiny notice picks up because the dates are on the contract note.
findings.market_standard: ClearTax, Zerodha's tax P&L, Winman and the ITD utility all classify on exact dates — 'held for more than 12 months' means more than 365/366 days from the day after acquisition.
findings.suggested_fix: Classify on dates, not month counts: long-term when sale_date > purchase_date + relativedelta(months=threshold) (or the equivalent day arithmetic). Keep holding_months for display only, and replace the boundary test with day-precision cases.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Holding period is counted in whole calendar months with the day discarded (capital_gains_engine.py:103-104), so a sale one day short of the twelve- or twenty-four-month anniversary is classified long-term and taxed at the LTCG rate. §2(42A) counts from the date of acquisition, so this is a wrong rate and a wrong gain_type written into the capital_gains register.
verification.probe: cd apps/api && python -c "compute_capital_gains('equity', date(2024,1,15), date(2025,1,5), 1_00_000_00, 3_00_000_00)" → months 12, is_long_term True, rate 12.5, section 'Section 112A', tax 937500 paise. Correct answer is STCG at 20% under §111A (356 days held). Property 15-Jan-2024 → 05-Jan-2026 likewise prints is_long_term True at 12.5% under 'Section 112 (Budget 2024)'.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed exactly. capital_gains_engine.py:103-104 holding_months(purchase, sale) = (sale.year-purchase.year)*12 + (sale.month-purchase.month) — the day of month is never read. :107-109 is_long_term compares that count with `>=` against 12 (equity) or 24 (other). compute_capital_gains:152-153 calls both, so a holding of 11 months and 21 days scores 12 and is classified long-term.
lens_notes.guards: None — the opposite. tests/test_capital_gains_engine.py:38-40 and :43-46 pin `is_long_term('equity', 12) is True` / `is_long_term('property', 24) is True` at month granularity, and :49-51 pins holding_months' whole-month arithmetic, so the suite locks the defect in. routers/income_tax.py:308-315 validates only that sale_date >= purchase_date; there is no day-level check anywhere.
lens_notes.reach: Live on both paths. POST /api/income-tax/capital-gains/compute (routers/income_tax.py:337) and POST /api/income-tax/capital-gains (:385) both call compute_capital_gains, and _cg_response:322 writes gain_type = 'LTCG'/'STCG' into the persisted register. findings.title: The ITR deadline tracker conflates assessment year with financial year — the period it stores and the due date it stores are a year apart
findings.evidence: apps/web/app/income-tax/page.tsx:62-67 `AY_PERIOD` maps '2025-26' to 2025-04-01 … 2026-03-31, which is FY 2025-26, i.e. AY 2026-27. Lines 69-79 then map the same key '2025-26' to due dates 2025-10-31 / 2025-07-31, which are the AY 2025-26 dates. Both are written into one compliance_calendar row at :509-519 (period_start/period_end from AY_PERIOD, due_date from the DUE_DATE_* maps). getAYFromDates (:95-100) derives the displayed 'AY' from the period start, so the column labelled Assessment Year actually shows the FY.
findings.ca_experience: A CA adds an ITR deadline for a client, picks '2025-26', and gets a row covering 1 Apr 2025 – 31 Mar 2026 that is due 31 July 2025 — four months before the year it covers has ended. Either the deadline is a year early or the period is a year wrong; on a dashboard whose whole job is to say what is due when, the row cannot be trusted either way, and 'overdue' badges fire against it (:597).
findings.market_standard: Every practice-management calendar keys ITR obligations on the AY and derives the previous year from it, so the two can never disagree. compliance_engine.itr_due_date already does exactly this on the backend and the page does not call it.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete the two hardcoded maps, call the backend for the period and the due date (compliance_engine.itr_due_date), and label the picker consistently — either AY throughout or FY throughout.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The page stores an FY-shaped period with an AY-shaped due date in one compliance_calendar row (app/income-tax/page.tsx:62-79, :508-519), and the backend seeder writes the opposite, correct pairing into the same table (routers/compliance.py:149-153), so the ITR list mixes rows whose due dates for the same displayed 'AY' are a year apart. One nuance the finding overstates: on screen the AY column round-trips (getAYFromDates(2025-04-01) = '2025-26' = the label picked), the period dates are never displayed, and the due date is editable — so the visible symptom is a default due date a year early and rows that disagree with seeded ones, not a self-evidently contradictory row.

findings.title: The presumptive engine for §44AD, §44ADA and §44AE is reachable from nothing — no endpoint, no request field, no screen

findings.title: No §54/§54F/§54EC/§54B reinvestment exemptions and no §112A grandfathering under §55(2)(ac)
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/capital_gains_engine.py computes gain = sale − cost − improvement (:139) and applies a rate; there is no exemption parameter, no CGAS deposit concept, and no 31-01-2018 fair-market-value input anywhere in the file or in routers/income_tax.py's ComputeCapitalGainsRequest (:299-306). `grep -rni '54F|54EC|55(2)(ac)|31-01-2018|grandfather' apps/api/domain/income_tax` finds only the Budget-2024 property indexation comment.
findings.ca_experience: Every property sale in an SME practice involves §54 or §54F, and every long-held listed equity holding involves the 31-01-2018 grandfathered cost. Without them the CA is shown the gross gain: on shares bought in 2012 and sold now the LTCG can be overstated by the entire pre-2018 appreciation, and on a house sold and reinvested the tax shown is the full 12.5% when the correct answer may be nil.

findings.title: §80CCD(2) is capped at 10% of salary for a non-government employee under the NEW regime, where the limit has been 14% since Finance (No.2) Act 2024

The direction is conservative, but it is still a wrong figure a CA cannot override.
findings.market_standard: greytHR, Zoho Payroll, RazorpayX Payroll and every ITR utility apply 14% under §115BAC(1A) and 10% under the old regime for non-government employees, and 14% for government employees in both.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the cap regime-dependent — 14% under §115BAC(1A) for everyone, 10% under the old regime for non-government employees — after confirming against the Finance (No.2) Act 2024 text, and change the pinning test with it.

findings.title: The ITR filing workflow offers only ITR-3/5/6/7, has no revised or updated return path, and the acknowledgement endpoint bypasses its own state machine
findings.evidence: apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/filing/page.tsx:43 `const ITR_FORMS = ["ITR-3", "ITR-5", "ITR-6", "ITR-7"]` — no ITR-1/2/4, although domain/income_tax/itr_json.py:114-282 holds verified field mappings for all seven. domain/income_tax/itr_workflow.py:22-28 makes 'filed' terminal with no outgoing transitions, and record_filing_acknowledgement (:212) writes status='filed' directly with no check of the current status, so a draft can be marked filed without review or partner review. routers/itr_workspace.py:70 takes itr_form as a free string with no validation, and assessment_year as a bare `str` while financial_year is an FYLabel. `grep -rni '139(8A)|139(5)|ITR-U|updated return' apps/api apps/web` returns nothing.
findings.ca_experience: A salaried or presumptive client cannot have a filing record created at all. Once a return is filed, a revised return under §139(5) or an updated return under §139(8A) — with its 25/50/60/70% additional tax after the Finance Act 2025 extension to 48 months — has nowhere to live, so the second-most-common ITR job in a practice is off the system. And the 'Partner review mandatory before Ready for Filing' promise on apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/page.tsx is not enforced on the acknowledge path.
findings.market_standard: Winman and CompuTax carry original/revised/updated as a return TYPE on the same client-year, prefill the revised return from the original acknowledgement number and date, and compute the §140B additional tax for ITR-U.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate itr_form against a Literal of all seven; add a return_type (original/revised/updated) and allow a filed return to spawn a revised one; make record_filing_acknowledgement require status == 'ready_for_filing'; type assessment_year.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The backend and the database both accept all seven ITR forms, and only the client screen restricts the list to four (filing/page.tsx:43) — a backend capability reachable from no screen, which confirms the gap. There is no return_type anywhere and the UNIQUE (firm_id, client_id, financial_year, itr_form) constraint (migration 319:111) actively prevents a §139(5)/§139(8A) return being recorded beside the original. The state-machine bypass in record_filing_acknowledgement (itr_workflow.py:212-249) is real but is gated in the UI to 'ready_for_filing' and by Manager+ RBAC, so it is a hardening item rather than the live hole the finding implies.

findings.title: The Form 26AS parser is fixed-column and silently drops every line it cannot read, then marks the upload 'parsed'
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/form26as_service.py:145-185 — the parser splits each line on tab or pipe, skips anything with fewer than five columns (:167), and reads deductor/TAN/date/amount/TDS from fixed positions 1..6. The whole record build is inside `try: … except (ValueError, IndexError): _logger.debug(...)` (:181-183), so a malformed row is dropped with a debug log and nothing else. `grep -n parse_errors form26as_service.py` shows it is initialised to [] at :85 and never written. save_parsed_records (:230) sets parse_status='parsed' regardless of how many records came out — including zero.
findings.ca_experience: A CA pastes a real 26AS (TRACES issues it as a password-protected PDF whose text dump is not tab-delimited in that column order) and the upload reports 'parsed'. If nothing matched the shape, total_records is 0 and the subsequent reconciliation then reports every book credit as 'not in 26AS' — the CA is told the client's whole TDS credit is unsupported and cannot be claimed. Nothing on screen says the parse found nothing.
findings.market_standard: ClearTax and TaxCloud ingest the TRACES text file and the PDF, validate the header and the section structure, and refuse an unrecognised file by name rather than producing an empty success.
findings.suggested_fix: Populate parse_errors with the skipped lines and the reason; refuse (parse_status='failed') when zero records are extracted or when the header does not identify a 26AS; and surface the count and the errors on the 26AS screen.

verification.what_is_actually_true: A 26AS dump that is not tab- or pipe-delimited in the expected column order parses to zero records, is stored as parse_status='parsed' with parse_errors=[] (form26as_service.py:274-279), and the reconciliation then reports the client's entire book TDS credit as unsupported. findings.title: The ITR due date is chosen by entity type rather than by whether an audit applies, so a small firm or LLP is given 31 October and an individual with a tax audit is given 31 July
findings.evidence: apps/web/app/income-tax/page.tsx:81-92 — AUDIT_ENTITY_TYPES contains private_limited, public_limited, llp, partnership, trust, aop, boi, and isAuditCase() returns true for any of them; handleAddFormChange (:488-492) picks DUE_DATE_AUDIT for those and DUE_DATE_NON_AUDIT for everyone else. Explanation 2 to §139(1) fixes 31 October for a company and for any OTHER person whose accounts are required to be audited — which turns on the §44AB turnover test, not on the legal form. The turnover is not consulted here at all, and the tax_audits table that records it lives on a different screen with no link.
findings.ca_experience: A partnership firm or LLP with ₹40 lakh turnover is given a 31 October deadline when its return is due 31 July; the client files late and picks up §234A interest and, under §80, loses the right to carry forward the year's business loss. An individual proprietor with ₹3 crore turnover — an audit case — is given 31 July when the correct date is 31 October, so the dashboard shows 'overdue' for three months on a return that is not.
findings.market_standard: Practice calendars in Winman, CompuTax and ClearTax Practice derive the ITR date from the audit flag on the client-year, which is itself set by the §44AB test, and companies are handled as their own case.
findings.suggested_fix: Take the audit flag from the client-year (the tax_audits row or a computed §44AB result), keep companies as an unconditional 31 October, and call compliance_engine.itr_due_date on the backend instead of the two hardcoded maps.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The prefill is derived from legal form, not from whether §44AB applies (income-tax/page.tsx:80-93, 483-491), so a non-audit LLP/partnership/trust is defaulted to 31 October and an audited proprietor to 31 July — but it is an editable field with the statutory rule labelled next to it, so it is a wrong default rather than an unavoidable wrong date. Worth adding: the backend's own generator has the same defect in the opposite direction — services/compliance_obligation_service.py:398 calls _itr_obligation(financial_year) with is_audit defaulting to False (:329-332), so every auto-generated ITR obligation is dated 31 July regardless of audit, even though compliance_engine.itr_due_date (services/compliance_engine.py:225-231) takes the flag correctly.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed. apps/web/app/income-tax/page.tsx:80-93 — AUDIT_ENTITY_TYPES = {private_limited, public_limited, llp, partnership, trust, aop, boi} and isAuditCase() tests membership only; handleAddFormChange (:483-491) sets due_date = DUE_DATE_AUDIT[ay] or DUE_DATE_NON_AUDIT[ay] purely from that set. findings.title: The §10(13A) HRA exemption is folded into Chapter VI-A 'total deductions' and gross total income is reported gross of it
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/itr_engine.py:360-363 adds `hra_exempt` to the same `deductions` accumulator as §80C/§80D/§80G, and :375 assigns that total to result.total_deductions_paise; the gross total income at :318 is computed BEFORE the exemption is removed. domain/income_tax/itr_json.py:355-356 then maps total_deductions to 'Deductions under Chapter VI-A' / 'Schedule VI-A' on every form. Probe: salary ₹10,00,000 old regime with a ₹2,00,000 HRA exemption → gross_total_income_paise ₹9,50,000 (i.e. gross of the exemption), total_deductions ₹2,00,000, taxable ₹7,50,000.
findings.ca_experience: The final tax is right, but the computation sheet the CA hands the client shows a gross total income ₹2 lakh too high and a Chapter VI-A figure ₹2 lakh too high. §10(13A) is an exemption computed in Schedule S before salary reaches GTI, not a Chapter VI-A deduction. If the payload is ever fed to the ITD utility, the ₹2 lakh lands in Schedule VI-A and the return will not validate against Schedule S.
findings.market_standard: Every computation sheet in the market shows HRA as a deduction from gross salary under §10(13A), above the standard deduction line, and never inside Chapter VI-A.
findings.suggested_fix: Deduct the HRA exemption from gross salary before the standard deduction, keep it out of the Chapter VI-A accumulator, and report it as its own line on the result and in the payload.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The classification error is real — §10(13A) (and §24(b)) are accumulated into total_deductions_paise (itr_engine.py:364-371) and GTI is struck before them (:316-318) — but the only live consequence is one inflated 'Total Deductions (Old Regime)' summary line on app/income-tax/deductions/page.tsx:539; the engine's GTI is rendered nowhere and the Schedule VI-A payload mapping in itr_json.py has no non-test caller.

findings.title: The §115BAC(6) regime-election engine — Form 10-IEA, the due date, the once-only withdrawal lock-out — is reachable from nothing; the screens carry a bare old/new dropdown
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/regime_election.py:145 evaluate_election is complete and covered by tests/test_regime_election.py, and is imported by no router (see IT-01 grep). The client workspace offers a two-option select (apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/computation/page.tsx:395-398 'New Regime (Default)' / 'Old Regime') and sends `use_new_regime` as a boolean; nothing asks whether Form 10-IEA was filed, when, or whether the option has already been withdrawn.
findings.ca_experience: The module's own docstring names the consequence: a missed Form 10-IEA taxes a business client on the new regime for a year they planned around the old one and cannot be cured after the §139(1) due date, and a withdrawal made without realising it is final closes the old regime permanently. A CA using this product picks 'Old Regime' from a dropdown and gets a number, with no prompt that a form is due and no record that the option has been spent.
findings.market_standard: Winman and CompuTax track the 10-IEA acknowledgement number and date on the client-year and warn when the old regime is selected without one, and carry the prior-year election history forward.
findings.suggested_fix: Expose evaluate_election behind /api/income-tax/regime-election, store the client's 10-IEA acknowledgement and prior elections, and gate the old-regime selection on the screen with the engine's own reasons rendered.

findings.title: §50AA is applied to every debt mutual fund regardless of acquisition date, and listed bonds and debentures are given the 24-month long-term threshold
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/capital_gains_engine.py:185-197 — the `_DEBT_MF_LIKE` branch charges a flat 30% estimate with no reference to purchase_date, while §50AA applies to specified mutual funds ACQUIRED on or after 01-04-2023; units acquired earlier are ordinary capital assets. capital_gains_engine.py:93-97 puts 'bonds' and 'other' in the 24-month bucket (_LONG_TERM_MONTHS_OTHER), whereas listed securities carry a 12-month threshold.
findings.ca_experience: A client's pre-April-2023 debt fund units are charged at a flat 30% slab estimate instead of being classified long-term, and a listed bond held 18 months is classified short-term. Both are wrong classifications that flow into the persisted register's gain_type and tax_rate_percent.
findings.market_standard: ClearTax and Zerodha's tax reports split debt funds at the 01-04-2023 acquisition boundary and hold a separate 12-month threshold for listed securities.
findings.suggested_fix: Branch the debt-MF path on purchase_date >= 2023-04-01; add a listed-security asset type with the 12-month threshold. Verify the post-23-07-2024 threshold table against the Act before writing it down.

verification.what_is_actually_true: A debt mutual fund unit acquired before 01-04-2023 is still routed through the §50AA branch and charged a flat 30% estimate (capital_gains_engine.py:184-196), and 'bonds' carries the 24-month threshold (:93-97), so a listed bond held 18 months is classified STCG. Both wrong classifications are persisted (gain_type / tax_rate_percent, routers/income_tax.py:415-420). The register's asset-type vocabulary has no listed/unlisted split, so fixing the second limb needs a new asset type, not just a threshold change.

findings.title: The Cost Inflation Index stops at FY 2025-26, so every indexed cost computed and STORED in the current financial year silently uses last year's index
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/capital_gains_engine.py:57-64 CII_BY_FY ends at '2025-26': 380, LATEST_CII_FY = '2025-26', and cii_for (:70-74) returns 380 for any later year with no flag on the result. routers/income_tax.py:353 create_capital_gains writes `result.indexed_cost_paise` into the capital_gains table. CapitalGainsResult (:118-134) has no 'index was estimated' field, and the endpoint response (_cg_response, :311) has none either. CLAUDE.md already records this as the one live instance of the fallback trap.
findings.ca_experience: A property gain computed today for FY 2026-27 uses CII 380 instead of the (not yet notified) 2026-27 index. The indexed cost is understated, the indexed gain overstated, and — unlike the tax figure, which the lower-of comparison usually rescues — the wrong indexed_cost_paise is persisted in the register and will be read back next year as if it were a fact.
findings.market_standard: Winman and ClearTax refuse to compute an indexed cost for a year whose CII CBDT has not notified, and say so, rather than substituting the previous year's number.
findings.suggested_fix: Have cii_for return a (value, is_estimate) pair or raise for an un-notified year; carry the flag through CapitalGainsResult and the API response; and refuse to PERSIST an indexed cost computed on an estimated index.

verification.what_is_actually_true: True, and the auditor understated it: the wrong index does not only corrupt the stored indexed_cost_paise, it can change the TAX. For immovable property capital_gains_engine.py:227-237 takes min(12.5% flat, 20% indexed); an understated indexed cost overstates the indexed branch, so the lower-of comparison picks the wrong branch. On a ₹50L 2015-16 purchase sold today for ₹1.20cr the shipped code returns ₹8,75,000 tax where a notified 2026-27 CII of 400 would give ₹8,25,196 — ₹49,803 too much — and persists an indexed cost of ₹74,80,314 instead of ₹78,74,015 (capital_gains_engine.py:158-159, routers/income_tax.py:414). Severity stays medium only because indexation now survives solely as the pre-23-Jul-2024 grandfathered option on immovable property.
verification.probe: cd apps/api && python -c "import domain.income_tax.capital_gains_engine as cg; ..." → 'as shipped (CII 380 substituted for 2026-27): indexed_cost=Rs 7480314 tax=Rs 875000' / 'if 2026-27 CII were 400: indexed_cost=Rs 7874015 tax=Rs 825196' / 'overstated tax = Rs 49803'. Also `cii_for('2026-27')` prints 380, and fy_for_date(2026-09-07) prints '2026-27'.

The opposite: apps/api/tests/test_capital_gains_engine.py:32-33 PINS the fallback (`assert cii_for('2030-31') == CII_BY_FY[LATEST_CII_FY]`), so the substitution is asserted as intended behaviour rather than caught. findings.title: Snapshots stay 'draft' forever — the review endpoint exists but no screen calls it, and the workspace's own 'partner review mandatory' promise is unenforced
findings.evidence: apps/api/routers/itr_workspace.py:196 POST /api/itr/snapshots/{id}/review is gated on rbac('income_tax','approve') and sets status='reviewed' (computation_workspace.py:147). `grep -rn 'snapshots/.*review' apps/web/app` returns nothing. The client computation screen renders latestSnap.status with styling for 'reviewed' and 'finalized' (apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/computation/page.tsx:361-365) but offers no control to reach either. apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/page.tsx:96 tells the CA 'Partner review mandatory before marking Ready for Filing'.
findings.ca_experience: Every computation in the product is permanently a draft. A partner cannot sign off a computation, a manager cannot see which computations have been reviewed, and the maker-checker discipline the product advertises exists only in the API. In a firm where an executive prepares and a partner signs, there is no record of who approved the number that went on the return.
findings.market_standard: Practice tools (ClearTax Practice, Winman's multi-user setup) put a two-step preparer/reviewer sign-off on the computation itself, with the reviewer's name and timestamp printed on the sheet.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a Review button on the computation screen calling the existing endpoint, show reviewer and timestamp on the snapshot card, and block the filing workflow's ready_for_filing transition unless the pinned snapshot is reviewed.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The snapshot-review endpoint is genuinely dead from the UI, so a computation snapshot's status is permanently 'draft' — but the auditor's consequences are wrong. The 'Partner review mandatory before marking Ready for Filing' line at apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/page.tsx:96 is about the ITR FILING workflow, which is enforced in itr_workflow.py:23-29 and driven from apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/filing/page.tsx:27,161-177, and partner_reviewed_by/partner_reviewed_at are recorded (itr_workflow.py:155-156). The one real residual gap is the third clause of the suggested fix: transition_itr_status never checks that the filing's computation_snapshot_id points at a reviewed snapshot. Downgraded to low — a stale status chip, not an absent maker-checker.

findings.title: 26AS reconciliation never feeds the computation — the TDS credit on the return is a number the CA retypes by hand
findings.evidence: The reconciliation compares 26AS against `receipts.tds_paise` (apps/api/domain/income_tax/form26as_service.py:56 BOOKS_SOURCE) and produces matched/mismatch/missing counts and an unsupported_credit_paise figure. Nothing writes a TDS total back: ITRComputeRequest.tds_deducted_paise (domain/income_tax/itr_engine.py:230) is a plain input, and the client computation screen collects it from a free-text field (apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/computation/page.tsx:105, sent at :230). There is no endpoint returning 'claimable TDS for this client-year'.
findings.ca_experience: A CA who has just run the 26AS reconciliation and knows exactly which credits are supported must then type the total into a different tab, by hand, with no check that the two agree. For a salaried client whose 26AS Part A credit never touches the receipts ledger, the reconciliation cannot see the credit at all, so the CA is on their own.
findings.market_standard: ClearTax and Winman prefill Schedule TDS-1/TDS-2 straight from the imported 26AS, per deductor and per TAN, and flag any credit claimed that 26AS does not support under Rule 37BA(1).
findings.suggested_fix: Return a claimable-TDS total (and a per-deductor schedule) from the reconciliation, and prefill the computation's TDS field from it with a visible variance if the CA overrides.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The gap is real: nothing computes a claimable-TDS figure or prefills the computation, and ITR TDS is hand-typed with no variance check (itr_engine.py:206; computation/page.tsx:105,410,230). The finding's 'no endpoint returning claimable TDS' is too strong — GET /api/form-26as/reconciliation already returns total_tds_26as_paise, unsupported_credit_paise and a per-deductor/per-TAN breakdown (form26as_service.py:468-515, routers/form_26as.py:195). The salaried-client point stands: _load_book_credits reads only `receipts` rows with tds_paise > 0 (form26as_service.py:371-380), so §192 salary credit has no books counterpart at all. Medium is right.
verification.probe: grep -rn 'claimable|prefill|tds_credit' over routers/form_26as.py, routers/income_tax.py, routers/itr_workspace.py → one hit, a comment. grep -n 'tds' apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/computation/page.tsx → useState('') at 105, label 'TDS Deducted (₹)' at 410.

The books side of the reconciliation is receipts.tds_paise only — apps/api/domain/income_tax/form26as_service.py:341-408 reads `receipts` joined to `customers` for the TAN, and BOOKS_SOURCE = 'receipts.tds_paise' at :54. On the computation side tds_deducted_paise is a plain input at domain/income_tax/itr_engine.py:206 (the finding cites :230; the field is at :206) and only feeds result.tds_and_advance_paise at :452. The frontend collects it as free text: apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/computation/page.tsx:105 useState(''), rendered as a bare '₹' field at :410, sent at :230 and :253. Nothing reads the reconciliation on that path.
lens_notes.guards: No guard, and no cross-check. The imprecision: the raw figures DO exist and ARE fetchable — summarise() at form26as_service.py:468-515 emits total_tds_26as_paise, unsupported_credit_paise and a per-deductor list carrying label/tan/total_26as_paise/variance, and GET /api/form-26as/reconciliation (routers/form_26as.py:195-207) returns it. lens_notes.reach: Reaches a user. Both screens are live and separately linked from apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/page.tsx:13 (computation) and :27 (26AS), so the CA does have to carry the number across two screens by hand.

findings.title: The Chapter VI-A surface stops at seven sections — no §80E, §80EE/EEA, §80DD/DDB, §80U, §80GG, §80JJAA, and no free-text §80C 'other' bucket through the API
findings.evidence: apps/api/domain/income_tax/itr_engine.py:24-80 defines limits for §80C, §80CCD(1B), §80CCD(2), §80D, §80TTA/TTB and §24(b) only; everything else has to go through the untyped `other_deductions_paise` (:225), which is added with no limit and no section attribution (:371). Deductions80C has an `other_paise` field (:100) that routers/income_tax.py:33-42 S80CInput does NOT expose, so §80C items like a five-year term deposit, stamp duty or §80CCD(1) cannot be entered at all through the API. §80D has no ₹5,000 preventive health check-up sub-limit and no medical-expenditure route for an uninsured senior.
findings.ca_experience: An old-regime individual with an education loan (§80E), a disabled dependant (§80DD), a specified illness (§80DDB) or no HRA but paying rent (§80GG) has to be lumped into one unlabelled 'other deductions' figure with no cap check and no line on the computation sheet. The CA loses the audit trail for exactly the deductions most likely to be questioned.
findings.market_standard: Winman, CompuTax and ClearTax present the full Chapter VI-A list with each section's own limit, sub-limits and evidence prompts, and print Schedule VI-A line by line.
findings.suggested_fix: Model the remaining Chapter VI-A sections with their own limits and a per-section result line (the tax_deduction_claims table already has a `section` column ready for it), and expose Deductions80C.other_paise on S80CInput.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The Chapter VI-A surface really does stop at §80C/§80CCD(1B)/§80CCD(2)/§80D/§80G/§80TTA-TTB plus §10(13A) and §24(b); §80E, §80EE/EEA, §80DD, §80DDB, §80U, §80GG and §80JJAA are absent from the whole income_tax domain, and §80D has neither the preventive-checkup sub-limit nor the uninsured-senior medical-expenditure route (itr_engine.py:108-119). Deductions80C.other_paise is unreachable through the API (routers/income_tax.py:32-42, :135-141). The one factual error is the five-year term deposit, which is supported as fd_5yr_paise. Add to the finding: the untyped other_deductions_paise fallback is added with no limit at itr_engine.py:374, so anything §80C routed through it escapes the §80CCE ₹1.5L cap.
verification.probe: grep -rn '80E\b|80EE|80EEA|80DD|80DDB|80U|80GG|80JJAA' apps/api/domain apps/api/routers apps/web/app/income-tax → 3 hits, all docstrings/comments naming the range, no implementation.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed except one example. apps/api/domain/income_tax/itr_engine.py:23-79 defines limits for §80C, §80CCD(1B), §80CCD(2), §80D, §80TTA/TTB, §24(b) and §71(3A) only; a repo-wide grep for 80E/80EE/80EEA/80DD/80DDB/80U/80GG/80JJAA across apps/api/domain, apps/api/routers and apps/web/app/income-tax returns no implementation — only three docstring mentions of the range '80C–80JJAA'. WRONG EXAMPLE: a five-year term deposit IS supported — fd_5yr_paise at itr_engine.py:96 and routers/income_tax.py:39.

The auditor's structural note checks out: public.tax_deduction_claims has a NOT NULL `section TEXT` column (apps/api/migrations/156_missing_tables_f5.sql:155).

The backend derives the schedule from the FY at apps/api/domain/income_tax/advance_tax_interest_engine.py:87-95 installment_schedule(fy) and compliance_engine.advance_tax_due_dates(:357), neither of which this page calls.

It is a display panel rather than a computation, so no money is wrong — but it is the first thing on the page and it is stale, which undermines confidence in everything below it.
findings.market_standard: Every compliance dashboard derives instalment dates from the selected year.
findings.suggested_fix: Derive the four dates from the selected FY (or call compliance_engine.advance_tax_due_dates) instead of the literal list.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Literally true, and slightly worse than described: not only the four dates but the panel's heading are hardcoded to FY 2025-26 (apps/web/app/income-tax/page.tsx:121-126 and :964), so today the tab is titled with last year and shows four elapsed instalments with no upcoming one. findings.title: The deductions planner fires two RBAC-gated compute calls on every debounced state change, including fields that cannot affect tax
findings.evidence: apps/web/app/income-tax/deductions/page.tsx:222-283 — one useEffect keyed on the whole `state` object runs `Promise.all([computeITR(old), computeITR(new)])` behind a 400 ms debounce; the dependency array is `[state]` (:283), which changes when a donation's description is typed, and the comment at :226-229 acknowledges this. Each call is a POST to /api/income-tax/compute on a Render Singapore instance that cold-starts.
findings.ca_experience: Typing a donation description or toggling a checkbox re-runs both regime computations. On a cold instance the CA watches the comparison panel blank and repopulate repeatedly while typing.
findings.market_standard: Desktop tools (Winman, CompuTax) compute locally and instantly; web tools compute on an explicit action or on a narrowed dependency set.
findings.suggested_fix: Key the effect on the tax-relevant fields only (a derived request object), or move to an explicit Recompute action.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The over-firing is real and self-documented: the effect is keyed on the whole `state` object (deductions/page.tsx:283) and a donation description is in it (:467), so a tax-irrelevant keystroke costs two cross-region compute calls after each 400 ms pause. The ca_experience is overstated — nothing blanks; the tax figures persist and only the recommendation line shows 'Computing…' (:558-561) while Save is disabled (:571). Low is correct; this is polish, not a defect a CA would report.

lens_notes.literal: Confirmed. apps/web/app/income-tax/deductions/page.tsx:224-283 is one useEffect whose dependency array is `[state]` (:283); inside, a 400 ms setTimeout fires Promise.all([computeITR(old), computeITR(new)]) (:266-271). A donation description is part of `state` — the input's onChange at :467 does upd({ donations: ds }) — so typing it does re-key the effect, exactly as the comment at :221-223 admits.
lens_notes.guards: Partly guarded, more than the finding allows. The 400 ms debounce plus the `cancelled` flag and clearTimeout in the cleanup (:282) mean continuous typing fires NO request at all; a pair of calls fires once per 400 ms idle pause, and any in-flight result from a superseded state is discarded. Both endpoints are stateless POSTs behind rbac('income_tax','compute') (apps/api/routers/income_tax.py:112-115) — nothing is written.
lens_notes.reach: Reachable (linked from apps/web/app/income-tax/page.tsx:744), but the described symptom does not occur. The comparison panel does not blank: the two regime cards at :544-555 keep rendering the previous oldResult/newResult while `computing` is true; only the recommendation strip swaps to 'Computing…' (:558-561) and the Save button disables (:571).

maturity.rationale: The domain layer is genuinely strong in places — FY-versioned statutory rates with a `verified` flag and correct FY 2025-26 slabs, rebate, marginal relief and surcharge caps in both regimes (probed and confirmed); a §234C engine that gets the fixed-period and trigger-tolerance structure right where the frontend it replaced got it wrong; ITR JSON field paths resolved against the Department's own committed schemas and pinned by tests; and several modules that REFUSE rather than guess (§32 depreciation in the bridge, the software-provider id, the presumptive under-declaration case). But the product a CA can actually reach is far behind that layer. Seven of the best-written modules — entity_rates, minimum_tax, presumptive, regime_election, book_to_tax_bridge, itr_json, itr_schema — are imported by no router and no screen, verified by grep this session. The one computation endpoint only computes individual slabs, which fits none of the described live client book. The per-client computation screen collects five figures and no deductions at all. And four defects put a wrong money number in front of a CA today: a capital loss reducing slab tax, §80G with no qualifying limit, capital gains charged at Budget-2024 rates for pre-23-July-2024 transfers, and §234C charged to presumptive assessees. Tax audit is a tracker with no 3CD, AIS persists nothing, and §234A/234B reach no screen. The scaffolding, the discipline and the test culture are there; the module is not.
maturity.grade_rationale_short: strong domain layer, largely unreachable product
maturity.would_a_ca_buy_this_module_alone: No — a CA firm serving SMEs cannot compute a company, firm or LLP return at all here, cannot produce a Form 3CD, and cannot get from this product to a filed-elsewhere JSON; the individual path it does have omits every Chapter VI-A deduction on the client screen.

strengths: FY-versioned statutory rates done properly: apps/api/domain/income_tax/statutory_rates.py:108-160 holds the FY 2025-26 new-regime slabs (0/5/10/15/20/25/30 at 4/8/12/16/20/24 lakh), the ₹60,000 §87A rebate at ₹12 lakh with marginal relief granted ONLY under the new regime (the old-regime cliff is encoded as data on RebateRule, :51-64, which is legally correct), the 25% new-regime surcharge cap and the 15% capital-gains surcharge cap. Probed this session: ₹12L → nil, ₹12.1L → ₹10,400 (relief working), ₹6cr new regime → 25% surcharge, old regime → 37%. All integer paise.

The 'dead control' discipline at apps/api/routers/income_tax.py:225-250: GET /api/income-tax/financial-years exists precisely so a picker cannot offer a year the engine has no rates for, and apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/computation/page.tsx:176-193 leaves the picker EMPTY on a failed probe rather than guessing. This is the right instinct applied to a real past failure.

The §234C engine (apps/api/domain/income_tax/advance_tax_interest_engine.py:78-179) gets the structure right where the frontend it replaced got it wrong: the 12%/36% trigger tolerance on instalments 1 and 2, the fixed 3/3/3/1-month periods regardless of actual delay, and cumulative-by-due-date counting so a late lump payment still counts for later instalments. The header (:16-32) names the exact §234B-shaped bug it fixed.

ITR JSON field paths are CHECKED, not believed: apps/api/domain/income_tax/itr_schema.py:75-95 resolves a dotted path through the Department's own committed schema and asserts the leaf is an integer, and tests/test_itr_schema_paths.py re-verifies every path in FIELD_MAPPINGS on every run (271 tests across the income-tax modules pass in 0.75s). The recorded near-miss at itr_json.py:104-113 — TaxPayableOnDeemedTI (the §115JB/§115JC branch) instead of TaxPayableOnTI on ITR-5/6, which would have validated perfectly and reported the wrong tax — is exactly the class of error this machinery exists to catch.

Refusing by name rather than emitting something plausible: apps/api/domain/income_tax/itr_json.py:390-427 raises SoftwareProviderNotRegistered and ReturnIncomplete with the specific missing thing, and domain/income_tax/book_to_tax_bridge.py:22-38 refuses to default IT Act §32 depreciation to the Companies Act book charge because 'a bridge that reconciles and lies is worse than one that refuses to reconcile'. Both are the right call.

Two commonly-botched entity-tax rules are correct: apps/api/domain/income_tax/entity_rates.py:127-137 turnover_reference_fy looks TWO years back for the 25% company rate (not at the year being taxed), and :227-231 applies the §115BAA/§115BAB surcharge as a flat 10% from the first rupee rather than reusing the normal brackets. Both are named in the module docstring as the easy mistakes.

The §115JEE asymmetry is modelled deliberately: apps/api/domain/income_tax/minimum_tax.py:78-80 excludes firm and LLP from the ₹20 lakh AMT cushion, with the docstring explaining that extending it to firms 'silently zeroes the liability of every small LLP that claims §35AD'. The MAT/AMT credit under §115JAA/§115JD is recorded rather than dropped (:255-311).

Presumptive arithmetic is careful in the right places: apps/api/domain/income_tax/presumptive.py:152-158 tests the 5% cash threshold by cross-multiplication so no division rounds a taxpayer across the boundary, :195-241 refuses to declare BELOW the presumptive figure (§44AD(5)) rather than quietly reducing it, and :373-380 does §44AE in kilograms because ₹1,000 per ton is exactly ₹1 per kg.

Client-scope authorization has been swept properly: every row-addressed endpoint in routers/itr_workspace.py (:26-64) and routers/form_26as.py (:26-42) resolves the row and checks can_access_client before acting, and routers/income_tax.py:326-345 does the same for the capital-gains register — each with a comment naming the specific gap it closed. The 26AS 404 message is deliberately identical for missing, wrong-firm and unassigned so it is not an existence oracle.

Money parsing is disciplined across all seven tax screens: apps/web/app/clients/[id]/tax/computation/page.tsx:197-209 reads and validates all five figures BEFORE computing anything, with the comment 'a gross salary read as ₹1 because it was typed 12,00,000 would produce a return that is internally consistent and completely wrong'. paiseFromRupeeInput is used everywhere; no Math.round(parseFloat(x)*100) survives in this subsystem.

The ITR filing demo (apps/api/services/filing_demo/itr.py:1-116) is honest: gated on status == 'ready_for_filing', reads the pinned snapshot with an explicit fallback chain, states in as many words that PracticeSync has no ITR JSON generator, and carries the §140 verification rule (the taxpayer signs, never the CA) and the 30-day e-verification clock.
test_coverage_notes:
"Volume is good and quality is uneven in a specific, diagnosable way: the eleven income-tax test modules (test_itr_engine, test_capital_gains_engine, test_advance_tax_interest_engine, test_minimum_tax, test_presumptive_taxation, test_entity_tax_rates, test_regime_election, test_book_to_tax_bridge, test_itr_json, test_itr_schema_paths, test_statutory_rates) run 271 tests and all pass in 0.75s. But the coverage tracks the DOMAIN modules in isolation, and the best-tested modules are precisely the ones no router imports — entity_rates, minimum_tax, presumptive, regime_election and book_to_tax_bridge each have a full suite and zero production callers, so the suite is green about code a CA cannot run.

Not covered at all, and each is a live defect found this session: a negative capital-gains figure reaching the tax computation (IT-02); §80G above the 10%-of-adjusted-GTI qualifying limit (IT-03); any transfer dated before 23-07-2024 (IT-04) — test_capital_gains_engine.py has no date-sensitive rate test whatever; §234C for a §44AD/§44ADA assessee (IT-06); AMT surcharge for an individual rather than a firm (IT-07); the §111A/§112 basic-exemption absorption (IT-08).

Two tests actively PIN behaviour I believe is wrong. tests/test_itr_engine.py:301-307 test_capped_at_10_percent_for_non_government_employee asserts the 10% §80CCD(2) cap for a non-government employee under the NEW regime, which Finance (No.2) Act 2024 raised to 14% (IT-20) — the test will have to change with the fix. tests/test_capital_gains_engine.py:38-40 test_equity_12_months_is_long_term_boundary asserts is_long_term('equity', 12) is True against a month-count that discards the day of the month, so it locks in the classification bug at IT-14 rather than catching it; tests/test_capital_gains_engine.py:49-51 test_holding_months_counts_whole_months does the same for the helper.

On the frontend, apps/web/lib/income-tax/taxAuditThresholds.test.ts is the only test in this subsystem's UI layer and it tests two constants — not the business logic sitting beside them in app/income-tax/tax-audit/page.tsx:207-213 that decides business-vs-profession by amount. There is no test asserting that a screen sends every field the backend accepts, which is what would have caught the five-field computation payload (IT-05).

What IS worth keeping: test_itr_schema_paths.py is a genuinely good pattern — it fails if a FIELD_MAPPINGS path stops resolving against the committed schema or stops naming an integer leaf, so a mid-year schema revision cannot silently move a figure into the wrong field."
open_questions_for_owner: Which assessee classes must this module serve first? CLAUDE.md records a live book of 4 Private Limited, 1 LLP, 1 Partnership, 1 Proprietorship and zero individuals, yet the only computation endpoint computes individual slabs. Should the next block of work be 'wire up entity_rates + minimum_tax and make the client screen compute a company', or 'finish the individual path'? The two are different quarters of work and the second serves nobody currently on the book.

Is Form 3CD in scope? A CA firm serving SMEs earns a large share of its income from §44AB tax audits, and the product holds none of the report — only a tracker row with a UDIN field. 3CD is a several-month build that would draw on the ledger, the disallowance workspace, the TDS module and GST. Is it a pillar you want, or is it deliberately out of scope?

How far back must the product compute? Belated, revised and updated returns mean FY 2023-24 and FY 2024-25 are live work, and the rate registries hold only 2025-26 and 2026-27 while the capital-gains engine has no notion of the 23-07-2024 rate change. Adding two or three past years to every registry is a bounded data job — is it worth doing, or should the product simply refuse a year it does not hold (which is what the /financial-years endpoint already does for the slab tables but not for capital gains)?

Where should the §32 block-of-assets register live — inside the fixed-asset module or as a separate tax register? It is the largest single line in almost every business computation, it is prerequisite to a real book-to-tax bridge and to Clause 18 of 3CD, and nothing in the codebase computes it today. Building it inside routers/fixed_assets.py risks confusing two depreciation systems in one table; building it separately means the CA maintains two registers.

What is the intended relationship between the firm-level Deductions planner (/income-tax/deductions, which sends the full deduction surface and compares both regimes) and the per-client Tax Computation workspace (which sends five figures and saves the snapshot the filing workflow reads)? They compute different things about the same client and neither knows the other exists. Should the planner write into the snapshot, or should the workspace absorb the planner?

Should any of the ITD's own e-Return Intermediary route be pursued? docs/compliance/03 §1 sets out Type-2 ERI's four serial gates and flags that production access is limited to four whitelisted INDIAN static IPs while apps/api runs on Render in Singapore — a deployment problem, not a code one. Until that is answered, itr_json.generate_itr_json will keep refusing, and the realistic ceiling for this module is 'compute perfectly, key into the ITD utility by hand'. Is exposing itr_field_placements as a printable keying sheet the right interim target?

The Income-tax Act 2025 commences 1 April 2026 and, per docs/compliance/03, renumbers §139 to §263 among much else, while CLAUDE.md records that ITR-1..7 are NOT renumbered for AY 2026-27. domain/tds/vocabulary.py forked the TDS vocabulary for exactly this reason. Does the income-tax side need the same fork — and if so, when does the trigger fire, given the committed schemas are AY 2026-27 and the current FY is already 2026-27?

How much should the product refuse versus estimate? The house style so far is admirable — refuse a §32 figure, refuse an ITR JSON, refuse a state's PT slab. But the capital-gains engine estimates a slab rate at a flat 30% and falls back to a stale CII without flagging it, and the ITR engine silently allows an unlimited §80G.
